screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll learn to watch, alert, trace, and investigate performance problems in AWS. Monitoring is more than dashboards: it's a disciplined process of collecting meaningful metrics, setting tuned alarms, and drilling into traces and network logs when things go wrong. You will see how CloudWatch captures metrics and logs from EC2, RDS, ALB, Lambda and other services, and how dashboards let you correlate those signals across your stack. We'll cover how to design alarms that avoid noise but still alert on real degradations, and how to instrument distributed apps with AWS X-Ray to trace a single request end to end. For network issues, VPC Flow Logs provide the low-level visibility needed to diagnose rejected traffic, high bandwidth consumers, and unexpected east-west flows. Throughout, I’ll show concrete examples: building a simple web-app dashboard, creating a C P U alarm and testing it, inspecting an X-Ray service map to find slow database calls, and querying Flow Logs to find blocked packets. By the end you’ll have a practical workflow: start with a dashboard, use alarms to detect drift, trace to find hotspots, and use flow logs for networking root cause analysis. Consider: which of these tools would you reach for first when users report intermittent slow responses?

screens.title: Amazon CloudWatch Basics
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon CloudWatch is the central monitoring service for AWS that collects metrics, logs, and events from services and resources. For performance work, metrics are the first thing you inspect because they give time-ordered numeric signals like CPUUtilization for EC2, ReadIOPS for RDS, and Invocations for Lambda. A good initial step is to identify which metric most directly reflects the user experience for each component—for a web server it may be C P U or requests per second; for a database it may be connections and read latency. Misconception alert: metrics are not a complete picture by themselves; they can show that something changed but not always why. Logs provide context; events and traces provide causality. Example: if CPUUtilization spikes on an EC2 instance, that could indicate a need to right-size the instance, a runaway process, or a backend dependency causing retries. Practical tip: establish a baseline for each metric during normal operation, then tune alarm thresholds around deviations from that baseline to avoid noisy alarms. Key takeaway: CloudWatch centralizes telemetry—learn to pick the right metric for the right service, and use logs and traces to investigate the cause once a signal appears.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › CloudWatch Basics
Definition

CloudWatch collects metrics, logs, and events

Metrics are numeric time series. Logs give detailed context. Events provide state changes. Use them together to detect and diagnose performance problems.

Common metrics
  • EC2: CPUUtilization, NetworkIn/Out
  • RDS: ReadIOPS, DatabaseConnections
  • ALB: Latency, HealthyHostCount
Misconception
High-level metrics can hide short spikes or causation; always pair metrics with logs or traces to find root cause.
Key Takeaway

Start with the metric that best reflects user impact, then add logs and traces for context.

Example & How-to
Create a dashboard widget showing EC2 CPUUtilization and NetworkIn/Out for a web server. Observe normal baseline, then note deviations.
Metric: EC2 > Per-Instance Metrics > CPUUtilization
Statistic: Average
Period: 1 minute
Add to Dashboard: MyWebAppPerformanceDashboard

Inspect spikes and compare with ALB latency and RDS connections.
Try this
Establish a baseline for CPU over 24 hours before setting alarms.
Common Mistake
Setting alarms without considering normal diurnal traffic patterns causes false positives.

screens.title: Designing CloudWatch Dashboards
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a useful CloudWatch dashboard follows a simple process: decide what user-facing experience you want to protect, identify the most representative metrics, choose visualization types, and arrange widgets so correlation is immediate. Start by defining the KPI—page latency, error rate, or throughput. Next, pick supporting metrics from infrastructure: ALB latency and request count, EC2 C P U and network, RDS connections and read latency, or queue depth for SQS. Avoid adding every metric; dashboards that overload the viewer reduce actionable clarity. Example: for a web app dashboard, combine an ALB latency line chart, an EC2 C P U number widget, RDS connections line, and an SQS queue depth number. Arrange the ALB and EC2 widgets so you can quickly see if latency spikes coincide with C P U climbs. Misconception: dashboards are not static; they evolve as your application architecture changes. Regularly prune or add widgets when services are scaled or removed. Practical tip: include a small text widget with the dashboard purpose, owner, and runbook link so responders know how to act. Closing question: which two metrics would you pair first to find a backend-induced latency spike?

screens.title: CloudWatch Alarms: Tuning vs Noisy Alerts
screens.narratorSegment: CloudWatch Alarms are essential for proactive detection, but poorly configured alarms create noise and desensitize teams. An alarm has several settings that determine sensitivity: the metric and statistic, the period (aggregation window), threshold, and the number of datapoints or evaluation periods required to alarm. If you set a very short period and require only one datapoint, transient spikes will trigger alerts. On the other hand, too long a period or too many datapoints can delay detection of real incidents. A practical approach is to establish a baseline and choose a threshold a reasonable percentage above that baseline, then choose period and datapoints that match how quickly you need to respond. Example: for C P U on a critical EC2 instance, you might set Average CPUUtilization >= 80 across a five-minute period with datapoints 1 out of 1 for quick detection in a test environment, or 3 out of 3 in production to avoid flapping during short spikes. Misconception: lower thresholds are always safer. In reality they often produce pager fatigue. Key takeaway: tune alarms around your application's normal behavior and adjust them after observing real traffic patterns.

keyIdea.title: Tune for signal, not noise

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Alarm Tuning
Comparison

Noisy alarm vs tuned alarm

Noisy Alarm
Short period, 1/1 datapoint, low threshold. Triggers on transient spikes, creates noise.
Tuned Alarm
Period and datapoints matched to traffic patterns, threshold set above baseline. Reliable and actionable.
Rule of thumb: test alarms in a staging environment with aggressive settings, observe behavior in production with conservative settings, then iterate. Use composite alarms to suppress noisy contributors when a higher-level signal is already triggered.
Example
An EC2 alarm configuration for production:
Metric: CPUUtilization • Statistic: Average • Period: 5 minutes • Threshold: 80 • Datapoints: 3/3
If immediate detection is required, lower datapoint count for a test alarm, but expect more false positives. Tune using historical data where possible.
Key Takeaway

Choose sensitivity that matches operational needs, and use composite alarms and automation to reduce human fatigue.

screens.title: Creating an Alarm: CLI Example
screens.narratorSegment: A practical way to create repeatable alarms is to use the AWS CLI. The CLI lets you script alarm creation and ensure consistency across environments. In the example shown visually, you will create a CloudWatch alarm for EC2 CPUUtilization and attach an SNS topic for notifications. The key parts are the metric name, namespace, statistic, period, threshold, and actions. Example CLI commands create an SNS topic, subscribe an email, and then create the alarm referencing that topic. Misconceptions to avoid: do not assume SNS subscription is immediate without confirmation; email subscriptions require confirmation. Also, remember region and IAM permissions—your CLI user needs permission to create topics and alarms. After creation, test the alarm in a safe way, such as in a staging instance where you can generate controlled C P U load. The reproducible script approach makes it simple to create identical alarms for multiple instances or to include alarm creation in infrastructure-as-code templates. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Alarm CLI Walkthrough
Code Walkthrough

Create SNS topic and alarm via CLI

# Create SNS topic
aws sns create-topic --name MySysOpsAlertsTopic

# Subscribe email (requires confirmation)
aws sns subscribe --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:... --protocol email --notification-endpoint you@example.com

# Create CloudWatch alarm for EC2 CPU
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name HighCPU_t3medium \
  --metric-name CPUUtilization \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 \
  --statistic Average \
  --period 300 \
  --threshold 80 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold \
  --evaluation-periods 3 \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:... \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-0123456789abcdef0
Explanation
This sequence creates a topic, subscribes an email that requires confirmation, and then creates an alarm referencing that SNS topic. The evaluation periods and threshold determine sensitivity.
Test tip
Generate load in staging with a stress tool to observe metric response and alarm firing.
Permissions
Ensure your IAM principal has sns:CreateTopic, sns:Subscribe, cloudwatch:PutMetricAlarm permissions.
Key Takeaway

Automate alarm creation so thresholds and actions are consistent and testable across environments.

screens.title: AWS X-Ray Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: AWS X-Ray provides end-to-end visibility for requests flowing through distributed applications. It collects traces that represent the path of a request through services—A P I Gateway, Lambda functions, EC2 hosts, and database calls—and presents a visual service map. The core idea is to see where time is spent and where errors occur on a per-request basis. A single spike in ALB latency might be due to a slow downstream database call; X-Ray lets you open a trace and inspect how long each segment took. Example: a request that shows a long segment for a particular Lambda function indicates the function itself or its downstream dependency is slow. Misconception: X-Ray complements but does not replace metrics. Use X-Ray when metrics and logs point to a distributed call that needs per-request analysis. Integration requires SDK instrumentation or agents; sampling is used to limit data volume. Practical tip: enable X-Ray in staging with higher sampling to understand typical traces, then reduce sampling in production to control cost. Key takeaway: X-Ray translates aggregate symptoms into a per-request story so you can find the slow component quickly.

keyIdea.text: Use tracing to convert metrics-level symptoms into actionable per-request insights and service-level hotspots.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › AWS X-Ray
Definition

X-Ray traces requests end-to-end

It records segments for service calls and shows a service map that highlights latency and error rates between components.
What you learn
Per-request timing, slow segments, and error origins across services.
Misconception
Tracing is not a replacement for metrics; it is the tool to use after a metric signals an anomaly.
Example
View a sample service map showing API Gateway → Lambda → RDS. One Lambda segment shows high latency. Inspect trace details to find the slow database call within the Lambda segment.
Integration
Use X-Ray SDK in application code or X-Ray agents where supported. Consider sampling to control trace volume.
Key Takeaway

Use X-Ray to convert an aggregated alert into a traceable request path and identify the slowest segment.

screens.title: Instrumenting Applications with X-Ray
screens.narratorSegment: Instrumenting your application to produce X-Ray traces requires adding the X-Ray SDK or enabling an agent depending on your runtime. For example, instrumenting Lambda functions often means adding the X-Ray SDK or enabling active tracing in the Lambda configuration so the platform will emit traces automatically for supported integrations. For services running on EC2, you can install the X-Ray daemon which receives local segment data and uploads traces to the X-Ray service. The pattern is consistent: capture a segment for each logical operation, record subsegments for external calls like database queries or HTTP requests, and propagate trace headers across service calls so fragments assemble into a single trace. Concrete example: a request that starts at A P I Gateway should include the trace header so when Lambda calls a database you see that database call nested under the Lambda segment. Misconception: more tracing does not always mean better debugging. Excessive instrumentation increases overhead and costs; use sampling and targeted tracing for critical paths. Closing takeaway: instrument with intent—trace the user-facing path and key downstream calls so you can find which service, function, or database is adding latency.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Instrumenting X-Ray
Architecture Pattern

Propagate traces across components

Key steps: enable tracing at entry points, record segments for operations, add subsegments for external calls, and forward trace headers between services.
Lambda
Enable active tracing or add SDK to record segments and annotations.
EC2 / Containers
Run the X-Ray daemon and instrument app code with the SDK.
Concrete Example
API Gateway receives the request, passes trace header to Lambda; Lambda records a DB subsegment for a query. In X-Ray, the trace shows API Gateway → Lambda → RDS with timings for each segment.
Key Takeaway
Trace propagation is essential: without trace headers you cannot assemble the full request path across services.

screens.title: VPC Flow Logs Overview
screens.narratorSegment: VPC Flow Logs provide metadata about IP traffic to and from network interfaces in a VPC. They don't contain packet payloads but do record source and destination IPs, ports, protocol, packet and byte counts, and whether traffic was accepted or rejected. This makes Flow Logs ideal for diagnosing connectivity problems like traffic blocked by security groups or NACLs, identifying heavy bandwidth consumers, or spotting unusual traffic patterns that may indicate security issues. Example query: filter Flow Logs for action='REJECT' to find denied traffic that correlates to a connectivity complaint. Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › VPC Flow Logs
Definition

Flow Logs record IP traffic metadata

They capture fields like src/dst IP, ports, protocol, bytes, packets, and action (ACCEPT/REJECT). Useful for connectivity and bandwidth troubleshooting.
Use cases
  • Find security group or NACL blocks
  • Identify high-volume IPs or ports
  • Detect unusual outbound connections
Query Example
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter action = 'REJECT'
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 20
Publish Flow Logs to CloudWatch Logs to run quick queries, or to S3 and use Athena for larger forensic searches.
Key Takeaway

Use Flow Logs to determine whether problems are network-level before modifying application code or scaling compute.

screens.title: A Systematic Troubleshooting Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: A repeatable troubleshooting workflow shortens Mean Time To Repair. Begin at the highest level: a dashboard or user report that describes the symptom. Next, identify the affected KPI and related metrics that might explain the behavior—ALB latency, EC2 C P U, RDS connections, queue depth—then look for correlated spikes in time. If metrics point to a specific component, open traces for representative requests with X-Ray to see per-request latencies and errors. If traces indicate external calls are slow, inspect the downstream service or database. If the issue looks like connectivity or unexpected traffic, query VPC Flow Logs for REJECT actions or unusually high byte counts. Throughout, use alarms to surface anomalies and runbooks to guide response. Example: A latency spike correlates with a sudden increase in RDS read latency; X-Ray traces show many requests waiting on a single slow query. Misconception: it’s tempting to scale horizontally immediately; scaling may hide root causes and increase cost. Key takeaway: follow a disciplined path—observe, correlate, trace, and verify with network logs—so you find the real root cause and apply the correct fix. screens.title: Network Tools: Reachability Analyzer and Network Access Analyzer
screens.narratorSegment: VPC Flow Logs provide raw traffic metadata, but AWS also offers diagnostic tools like Reachability Analyzer and Network Access Analyzer to understand network paths and unintended access. Reachability Analyzer lets you simulate and test reachability between two resources and shows the virtual network path, identifying components that block traffic. This is useful when you suspect there is a path issue but need to see the sequence of components affecting it. Network Access Analyzer helps detect unintended access rules that might expose resources. Misconception: these tools replace Flow Logs. They do not. Use Reachability Analyzer to validate and visualize specific paths, use Flow Logs to observe actual traffic patterns over time, and use Network Access Analyzer to detect overly permissive policies. Example: if a service cannot reach a database, run Reachability Analyzer to see which security group or route table entry blocks the path; then confirm with Flow Logs whether traffic is being rejected. Key takeaway: combine diagnostic tools—use visual path analysis for configuration checks and Flow Logs for runtime evidence. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll learn to watch, alert, trace, and investigate performance problems in AWS. Monitoring is more than dashboards: it's a disciplined process of collecting meaningful metrics, setting tuned alarms, and drilling into traces and network logs when things go wrong. You will see how CloudWatch captures metrics and logs from EC2, RDS, ALB, Lambda and other services, and how dashboards let you correlate those signals across your stack. We'll cover how to design alarms that avoid noise but still alert on real degradations, and how to instrument distributed apps with AWS X-Ray to trace a single request end to end. For network issues, VPC Flow Logs provide the low-level visibility needed to diagnose rejected traffic, high bandwidth consumers, and unexpected east-west flows. Throughout, I’ll show concrete examples: building a simple web-app dashboard, creating a C P U alarm and testing it, inspecting an X-Ray service map to find slow database calls, and querying Flow Logs to find blocked packets. By the end you’ll have a practical workflow: start with a dashboard, use alarms to detect drift, trace to find hotspots, and use flow logs for networking root cause analysis. Consider: which of these tools would you reach for first when users report intermittent slow responses?

These four objectives map to concrete SysOps skills you will practice. First, you’ll learn to use CloudWatch to collect and interpret service metrics and logs. This matters because the right metric tells you where to look when performance drifts. Second, you will create custom CloudWatch dashboards to visualize KPIs across services. Dashboards let you correlate signals like ALB latency and database connections, reducing time to detect multi-service issues. Third, you will configure CloudWatch Alarms to notify or automatically respond when thresholds are crossed. Tuning those alarms avoids distracting noise and ensures fast human or automated remediation. Fourth, you’ll apply AWS X-Ray and VPC Flow Logs to trace distributed requests and diagnose network-level problems. X-Ray helps you pinpoint slow functions or database calls; Flow Logs reveal rejected or high-volume traffic. Each objective includes a milestone: building a dashboard with EC2 C P U and network widgets, creating an alarm that triggers an SNS notification, instrumenting a Lambda with X-Ray, and querying Flow Logs for blocked traffic. These are practical, verifiable competencies you can use right away to reduce incident response time and improve availability.

This second objectives slide focuses on labable, testable outcomes. For CloudWatch metrics, you will identify the most relevant metrics for a given service—like CPUUtilization for EC2, ReadIOPS for RDS, or Invocations for Lambda—and show how to interpret sustained changes versus transient spikes. For dashboards, you will combine widgets—number, line, and text—into a single Web Application Performance dashboard so you can see correlated signals at a glance. For alarms, you will configure a C P U alarm with a threshold and SNS action, then test it by generating load. That practice demonstrates awareness of alarm periods and datapoints settings, which determine sensitivity. For distributed tracing and network diagnostics, you will instrument a function with X-Ray and view a service map to find the slowest segment, and query VPC Flow Logs to find REJECTed traffic or bandwidth-hogging IPs. Each exercise teaches a diagnostic pattern: start with the high-level dashboard, drill down to the offending metric, trace requests to find the code or service, and use Flow Logs to rule out network causes. These are the exact skills you'll perform in the hands-on activity that follows.

Amazon CloudWatch is the central monitoring service for AWS that collects metrics, logs, and events from services and resources. For performance work, metrics are the first thing you inspect because they give time-ordered numeric signals like CPUUtilization for EC2, ReadIOPS for RDS, and Invocations for Lambda. A good initial step is to identify which metric most directly reflects the user experience for each component—for a web server it may be C P U or requests per second; for a database it may be connections and read latency. Misconception alert: metrics are not a complete picture by themselves; they can show that something changed but not always why. Logs provide context; events and traces provide causality. Example: if CPUUtilization spikes on an EC2 instance, that could indicate a need to right-size the instance, a runaway process, or a backend dependency causing retries. Practical tip: establish a baseline for each metric during normal operation, then tune alarm thresholds around deviations from that baseline to avoid noisy alarms. Key takeaway: CloudWatch centralizes telemetry—learn to pick the right metric for the right service, and use logs and traces to investigate the cause once a signal appears.

Designing a useful CloudWatch dashboard follows a simple process: decide what user-facing experience you want to protect, identify the most representative metrics, choose visualization types, and arrange widgets so correlation is immediate. Start by defining the KPI—page latency, error rate, or throughput. Next, pick supporting metrics from infrastructure: ALB latency and request count, EC2 C P U and network, RDS connections and read latency, or queue depth for SQS. Avoid adding every metric; dashboards that overload the viewer reduce actionable clarity. Example: for a web app dashboard, combine an ALB latency line chart, an EC2 C P U number widget, RDS connections line, and an SQS queue depth number. Arrange the ALB and EC2 widgets so you can quickly see if latency spikes coincide with C P U climbs. Misconception: dashboards are not static; they evolve as your application architecture changes. Regularly prune or add widgets when services are scaled or removed. Practical tip: include a small text widget with the dashboard purpose, owner, and runbook link so responders know how to act. Closing question: which two metrics would you pair first to find a backend-induced latency spike?

CloudWatch Alarms are essential for proactive detection, but poorly configured alarms create noise and desensitize teams. An alarm has several settings that determine sensitivity: the metric and statistic, the period (aggregation window), threshold, and the number of datapoints or evaluation periods required to alarm. If you set a very short period and require only one datapoint, transient spikes will trigger alerts. On the other hand, too long a period or too many datapoints can delay detection of real incidents. A practical approach is to establish a baseline and choose a threshold a reasonable percentage above that baseline, then choose period and datapoints that match how quickly you need to respond. Example: for C P U on a critical EC2 instance, you might set Average CPUUtilization >= 80 across a five-minute period with datapoints 1 out of 1 for quick detection in a test environment, or 3 out of 3 in production to avoid flapping during short spikes. Misconception: lower thresholds are always safer. In reality they often produce pager fatigue. Key takeaway: tune alarms around your application's normal behavior and adjust them after observing real traffic patterns.

A practical way to create repeatable alarms is to use the AWS CLI. The CLI lets you script alarm creation and ensure consistency across environments. In the example shown visually, you will create a CloudWatch alarm for EC2 CPUUtilization and attach an SNS topic for notifications. The key parts are the metric name, namespace, statistic, period, threshold, and actions. Example CLI commands create an SNS topic, subscribe an email, and then create the alarm referencing that topic. Misconceptions to avoid: do not assume SNS subscription is immediate without confirmation; email subscriptions require confirmation. Also, remember region and IAM permissions—your CLI user needs permission to create topics and alarms. After creation, test the alarm in a safe way, such as in a staging instance where you can generate controlled C P U load. The reproducible script approach makes it simple to create identical alarms for multiple instances or to include alarm creation in infrastructure-as-code templates. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AWS X-Ray provides end-to-end visibility for requests flowing through distributed applications. It collects traces that represent the path of a request through services—A P I Gateway, Lambda functions, EC2 hosts, and database calls—and presents a visual service map. The core idea is to see where time is spent and where errors occur on a per-request basis. A single spike in ALB latency might be due to a slow downstream database call; X-Ray lets you open a trace and inspect how long each segment took. Example: a request that shows a long segment for a particular Lambda function indicates the function itself or its downstream dependency is slow. Misconception: X-Ray complements but does not replace metrics. Use X-Ray when metrics and logs point to a distributed call that needs per-request analysis. Integration requires SDK instrumentation or agents; sampling is used to limit data volume. Practical tip: enable X-Ray in staging with higher sampling to understand typical traces, then reduce sampling in production to control cost. Key takeaway: X-Ray translates aggregate symptoms into a per-request story so you can find the slow component quickly.

Instrumenting your application to produce X-Ray traces requires adding the X-Ray SDK or enabling an agent depending on your runtime. For example, instrumenting Lambda functions often means adding the X-Ray SDK or enabling active tracing in the Lambda configuration so the platform will emit traces automatically for supported integrations. For services running on EC2, you can install the X-Ray daemon which receives local segment data and uploads traces to the X-Ray service. The pattern is consistent: capture a segment for each logical operation, record subsegments for external calls like database queries or HTTP requests, and propagate trace headers across service calls so fragments assemble into a single trace. Concrete example: a request that starts at A P I Gateway should include the trace header so when Lambda calls a database you see that database call nested under the Lambda segment. Misconception: more tracing does not always mean better debugging. Excessive instrumentation increases overhead and costs; use sampling and targeted tracing for critical paths. Closing takeaway: instrument with intent—trace the user-facing path and key downstream calls so you can find which service, function, or database is adding latency.

Next, identify the affected KPI and related metrics that might explain the behavior—ALB latency, EC2 C P U, RDS connections, queue depth—then look for correlated spikes in time. VPC Flow Logs provide raw traffic metadata, but AWS also offers diagnostic tools like Reachability Analyzer and Network Access Analyzer to understand network paths and unintended access. Reachability Analyzer lets you simulate and test reachability between two resources and shows the virtual network path, identifying components that block traffic. This is useful when you suspect there is a path issue but need to see the sequence of components affecting it. Network Access Analyzer helps detect unintended access rules that might expose resources. Misconception: these tools replace Flow Logs. They do not. Use Reachability Analyzer to validate and visualize specific paths, use Flow Logs to observe actual traffic patterns over time, and use Network Access Analyzer to detect overly permissive policies. Example: if a service cannot reach a database, run Reachability Analyzer to see which security group or route table entry blocks the path; then confirm with Flow Logs whether traffic is being rejected. Key takeaway: combine diagnostic tools—use visual path analysis for configuration checks and Flow Logs for runtime evidence. Here are the core concepts to take away. First, CloudWatch is your foundational telemetry source: pick the right metric for the service and pair it with logs and traces for context. Second, dashboards should be minimal and designed for correlation so you can quickly see whether an infrastructure metric explains a user-facing symptom. Third, alarms must be tuned: choose period and datapoints that match your traffic patterns to reduce noise while keeping detection timely. These three ideas form the baseline of effective monitoring practice—metrics for signals, dashboards for context, and alarms for action.
